taxes.title: Taxes: nominal versus effective
taxes.lead: Two questions get mixed up constantly: what rate does the law prescribe, and what share of their economic gains do the very rich actually hand over? The answer depends entirely on the denominator, so this page always says which one is used.

definitions.title: Three definitions, never mixed
definitions.a: (a) Tax ÷ taxable income. What the tax return shows. Unrealised gains and retained corporate profits are not income here.
definitions.b: (b) Tax ÷ economic income, including unrealised gains and retained profits. The way economists measure how much richer someone got in a year.
definitions.c: (c) Tax ÷ wealth. Tax paid as a share of the stock of wealth. Used in the billionaire-tax debate.
definitions.corp: Each can be computed with or without corporate taxes attributed to the owner. A company's profits are taxed before they reach the shareholder; whether you count that as the owner's tax is a genuine choice, so both variants are shown.

nominal.title: Statutory rates, 2026
nominal.incomeNoteDe: 45 % above {threshold} taxable income, plus 5.5 % solidarity surcharge = 47.5 %.
nominal.incomeNoteUs: 37 % above {threshold} taxable income (single). State income taxes come on top and are not shown.
nominal.capitalNoteDe: 25 % flat withholding tax plus surcharge = 26.375 %. Only when paid out or sold.
nominal.capitalNoteUs: 20 % plus 3.8 % net investment income tax = 23.8 %. Only when sold; basis is stepped up at death.
nominal.corporateNoteDe: 15 % corporate tax + surcharge + trade tax at the average municipal multiplier ≈ 30 %. Corporate tax falls to 10 % by 2032.
nominal.corporateNoteUs: 21 % federal; state corporate taxes come on top.
nominal.inheritanceNoteDe: 7–30 % for spouses and children, up to 50 % for others, after allowances. Business assets can be 85–100 % exempt.
nominal.inheritanceNoteUs: 40 % above an exemption of {exemption} per person.
nominal.tradeTaxLine: Trade tax at the 2024 average municipal multiplier (409 %): {rate} of trade income, on top of the 15.825 % corporate tax including surcharge.

effective.title: What the very wealthy actually pay, according to research
effective.note: Rates in different rows are not comparable with each other unless denominator and corporate-tax treatment match. Wealth-based rates (c) look tiny because wealth is a stock, not a flow: 0.5 % of wealth can be a large share of one year's income growth — or a small one.

calc.title: What would you pay at a billionaire's rate?
calc.lead: Enter a gross annual income. The calculator applies the 2026 German income-tax tariff (or the US federal brackets) and, optionally, employee social contributions. Then it applies the effective rates from the research above to the same income. Wealth-based rates are applied to net wealth, never to income.
calc.yourRate: That is {rate} of your gross income.
calc.atRate: At {rate} ({who}) you would pay {money} instead of {actual}.
calc.wealthLead: The EU Tax Observatory measures billionaires' taxes as a share of their wealth. To compare fairly, apply that share to a median household's net wealth ({wealth}):
calc.wealthLine: {rate} of {wealth} = {money} per year ({who}). Your actual deductions: {actual}.
calc.assumptions: Assumptions: single, no children, no other income; Germany: employee lump sum of 1,230 € and social contributions deducted before tax, health insurance at the average supplementary contribution; USA: standard deduction, federal tax only, no state tax. Social contributions in the US are Social Security and Medicare employee shares. Rounded.
calc.socialNote: Social contributions buy pension, health and unemployment cover; whether to count them as ‘tax’ is contested, so both views are offered.

items.h: The wealth tax has been suspended since 1997
items.p: The Constitutional Court ruled in 1995 (2 BvL 37/91) that valuing real estate far below other assets violated equal treatment and gave the legislature until the end of 1996 to fix it. It did not. The Wealth Tax Act still exists but has not been applied since. Estimates of what a reintroduced tax could raise range from about 10–30 billion € (Netzwerk Steuergerechtigkeit, billionaire-only variant) to far more for broad variants (DIW).

items.h: Business assets are largely exempt from inheritance tax
items.p: Under §§ 13a and 13b ErbStG, business assets pass 85 % or even 100 % tax-free if the business is continued and payroll is maintained. In 2024 alone, exemptions under § 13a covered {exempt} of transferred assets while total inheritance and gift tax assessed was {assessed}. Very large transfers can additionally apply for a needs test or a reduction.

items.h: Retained profits in holdings and foundations
items.p: A person who holds a company through a holding company pays no personal tax on profits as long as they stay inside the holding; dividends between corporations are 95 % exempt (§ 8b KStG). The corporate-level tax of about 30 % is the whole bill until money is paid out. Family foundations can hold companies across generations and pay a substitute inheritance tax only every 30 years.

Whoever moves abroad while holding at least 1 % of a company is taxed as if they had sold those shares (§ 6 AStG). This limits the ‘they will just leave’ route for the largest fortunes, but it also creates lock-in and disputes over valuation and deferral.

objections.title: Objections, steel-manned
objections.lead: A site like this only convinces if it survives the best counter-arguments. Here they are in their strongest form, each with a data-based answer and an honest note on where it has a point.

paper.title: “It is not cash, it is paper wealth.”
paper.steelman: Nearly all of these fortunes are shares in one company. Nobody has {topWealth} in a bank account. If the owner tried to sell, the price would collapse; the number is a mark-to-market fiction that could halve in a bad year, as it did for several people in 2022.
paper.answer: True, and irrelevant for most of what wealth does. Shares can be borrowed against: banks lend against listed stock at low rates, which is how owners fund consumption without selling or paying capital gains tax (‘buy, borrow, die’). Elon Musk had pledged about 236 million Tesla shares as loan collateral according to Tesla's own filings, as reported by Handelsblatt. Shares also carry control over companies with hundreds of thousands of employees, and they pay dividends: BMW proposed {bmwDividend} per ordinary share for the 2025 financial year, and the Quandt/Klatten siblings, the largest shareholders, are the main beneficiaries. Cash is not what makes wealth powerful.
paper.core: Valuations move. This site shows the range across sources for that reason, and the fortunes shown are the current estimate, not a guaranteed sale price. A forced sale of a large stake would indeed fetch less.

valuation.title: “The valuations are unreliable.”
valuation.steelman: Forbes, Bloomberg and Manager Magazin all produce different numbers for the same person, sometimes 30 % apart. Private companies like Lidl or Aldi have no share price; their ‘value’ is a guess based on comparable listed firms. Debts, trusts and family agreements are often invisible.
valuation.answer: Correct, so every fortune here carries its source, its date and, where we have it, the range across sources; hover the ⓘ. For example, Forbes puts Dieter Schwarz at {schwarzForbes}, Manager Magazin at {schwarzMM}. But the uncertainty is a matter of tens of per cent, while the gap to a median household is a factor of hundreds of thousands. Whether the richest German owns 400,000 or 550,000 median households' worth changes nothing about the picture.
valuation.core: For private fortunes the error bars are wide, and rankings among the top ten should not be taken literally. Numbers with more than two significant digits suggest a precision that does not exist.

earned.title: “They earned it and took the risk; the money is in companies that create jobs.”
earned.steelman: Founders like Musk, Huang or the Albrechts built companies that employ millions and produce things people want. Their wealth is not taken from anyone; it is the market value of what they created. Taxing it means taxing the companies, the jobs and future innovation.
earned.answer: Two of the ten richest Germans built their companies; the others inherited them (Klatten, Quandt, Albrecht, Heister, Schaeffler, Merckle). Even for founders the return is not proportional to effort: returns of this size come from owning equity in a winner, which is a mix of skill, timing, luck and public goods such as roads, courts, education and research. And ‘the money is in companies’ argues against taxing the companies, not against taxing the owner: a 2 % tax on a founder's stake can be paid from dividends or a small sale without touching the firm, as the same owners already do for their own spending.
earned.core: Company-building is real and valuable, taxes on business substance can destroy it, and any wealth tax has to be designed so it hits the owner, not the working capital. That is a design constraint, not an argument against measuring the scale.

zerosum.title: “Wealth is not a zero-sum game.”
zerosum.steelman: When Tesla's share price rises, no one gets poorer. Fortunes grow because companies became more valuable, and everyone can hold shares. Comparing a billionaire to the median household implies the one took from the other, which is false.
zerosum.answer: Correct: the comparison does not claim theft. It claims scale. Wealth is not zero-sum, but its distribution still matters because wealth buys political influence, media, housing and land, of which there is a fixed amount, and because the poorer half of German households owns about {bottom50} of household wealth: they do not ‘hold shares’ in any meaningful amount. A non-zero-sum game can still leave half the players with almost nothing.
zerosum.core: Rising fortunes mostly reflect rising company values, not redistribution. Anyone who says ‘the rich took it from the poor’ is making a different claim than this site.

leave.title: “Tax them more and they will leave.”
leave.steelman: Capital is mobile. Norway raised its wealth tax in 2022 and dozens of wealthy Norwegians moved to Switzerland; the tax base shrinks and the country ends up with less revenue and fewer investors.
leave.answer: Norway is the best case for this objection, and the numbers are modest: {norwayLeavers} wealthy individuals left in 2022–2023 out of several thousand liable, and wealth-tax revenue rose sharply because the base is broad. The academic literature (Kleven, Landais, Muñoz & Stantcheva, Journal of Economic Perspectives 2020) finds that tax-driven migration exists but is small for most groups, especially where exit taxes exist. Germany taxes the unrealised gains of anyone who leaves with a stake of 1 % or more (§ 6 AStG), which makes emigrating with a company fortune expensive.
leave.core: Some people do move, and revenue estimates that ignore behaviour overstate what a tax will raise. Design matters: exit taxation, international coordination and valuation rules decide whether a tax works.

twopercent.title: “2 % of a billion is more than 45 % of 80,000 €.”
twopercent.steelman: In absolute terms the rich pay enormous sums. The top 10 % of earners pay {taxShare} of German income tax. A billionaire paying ‘only’ 2 % of a billion hands over 20 million €, which funds hundreds of teachers. The median earner's 45 % top rate is a headline; in absolute money it is nothing in comparison.
twopercent.answer: Both things are true. The absolute sums are large, and this site's spend simulator shows exactly how much a billion buys. Tax systems, however, are built on ability to pay: a rate, not an amount, because 45 % of 80,000 € changes how a family lives and 2 % of a billion changes nothing about how the owner lives. The relevant comparison is share of resources: the top 10 % pay {taxShare} of income tax while holding {top10share} of net wealth, and income tax does not reach wealth at all until it is sold. The ‘they already pay most of the income tax’ statistic is about income, and the fortunes on this site are not income.
twopercent.core: The absolute amounts are genuinely high, and any redistribution argument that pretends the rich pay nothing is wrong. Effective rates on the very top are lower than in the middle only under definitions (b) and (c); under definition (a) they are higher.

mittelstand.title: “German fortunes are family businesses and the Mittelstand.”
mittelstand.steelman: Unlike US tech founders, German wealth sits in Lidl, Aldi, BMW, Würth, Merck: long-lived, employee-heavy firms that reinvest and stay put. Taxing their owners threatens exactly the model that makes the German economy resilient.
mittelstand.answer: This is why this site marks family entries and shows per-person values where sources name the people. But ‘Mittelstand’ and ‘ten largest fortunes’ are different populations: the firms behind the top ten have tens or hundreds of thousands of employees and are among the largest companies in Europe. The inheritance-tax exemption for business assets (§ 13a ErbStG) exempted {exempt} in 2024, and the Destatis statistics show the largest exemptions go to the largest transfers, not to small firms.
mittelstand.core: Family ownership with long horizons is a real strength, and rules that force a sale to pay tax would damage it. Instalment and deferral rules exist for that reason; the question is whether an unlimited exemption is needed to protect it.

methodology.title: Methodology and sources
methodology.principle: Credibility before impact. Every figure on this site has a source, a retrieval date, a reference period and a definition, visible through the ⓘ button next to it. Estimates are marked with ≈. Where reliable data are missing, the site says so instead of guessing.

p: Bars are drawn at a configurable scale (default: one pixel = 1,000 in the display currency). Amounts are converted between US dollars and euros with the ECB daily reference rate ({rate} USD per EUR on {date}); the original currency is always shown in the tooltip.
Money ‘scrolled’ is the sum of all bars left of the viewport edge, not the pixel distance, because bars are separated by gaps.

Primary source for individual fortunes is the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires list, read once a month by the pipeline. The German top ten are the ten largest entries whose Forbes citizenship field says Germany, so people Forbes lists under another citizenship (for example Klaus-Michael Kühne in the real-time list) are missing and are noted separately.

Alternative estimates are attached per person: the Forbes annual list and, for Germans, the Manager Magazin list of October 2025 (taken from the Wikipedia snapshot because the magazine is paywalled). The tooltip shows the range. Rule for conflicts: the most recent reputable estimate is the headline; older or joint-family figures are shown as the range.
Family entries pool several people. A per-person value is shown only where a source names the people; otherwise the site says that no reliable data exist.

German median and mean household net wealth: Bundesbank Panel on Household Finances 2023. Median earnings: Destatis earnings survey. US household income: Census Bureau. US family net worth: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances 2022 (the 2025 wave was not yet published). Lifetime earnings in Germany are a transparent multiplication (median × 45 years) cross-checked with the IAB; in the US the Georgetown CEW estimate.

Every item in the spend simulator has a price year. Older prices can be rebased to the latest consumer price index year of their currency (Eurostat HICP for Germany, BLS CPI-U for the US); the switch is off by default and the tooltip always shows the original.

Statutory rates come from the law texts (gesetze-im-internet.de, IRS). Effective rates come from named studies, each tagged with its denominator ((a) taxable income, (b) economic income, (c) wealth) and whether corporate taxes are attributed to the owner. The calculator implements the 2026 German tariff formula (§ 32a EStG) and the 2026 US federal brackets with the stated simplifications.

A GitHub Actions workflow runs on the first of each month (and on demand). It fetches ECB rates, Eurostat HICP, BLS CPI and the Forbes lists, validates every file against a JSON schema, and commits only values that pass a plausibility check: a fetched value that deviates from the last known good value by more than {threshold} is not written but listed in an issue for review. Values that cannot be fetched automatically (surveys, studies, law parameters) carry a maximum age; when they exceed it, the same issue lists them with a hint where to find the update.
Every change is recorded in DATA-CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Wealth lists are estimates with wide error bars for private companies. Survey data under-cover the very top, so shares like ‘the poorer half holds 2.4 %’ are, if anything, generous to the top. Comparing a German full-time median earner with a US median household mixes an individual and a household measure; both are labelled. The tax calculator ignores state taxes in the US, church tax and children in Germany, and all deductions beyond the standard ones. Effective-rate studies are contested; the contest is summarised in the objections chapter.

credits.title: Credits
credits.lead: This site rebuilds and combines three well-known visualisations. Nothing was copied from them; every part was implemented from scratch and the data are new.

linkStatus.offline: original URL was offline when checked on {date}; the mirror link works

credits.korostoffNote: Matt Korostoff's site set 1 pixel = 1,000 $ and scrolled through the wealth of the 400 richest Americans. This site keeps his scale and format, adds virtual scrolling (browsers cannot render elements a billion pixels wide), euro conversion, German data and sourced tooltips.
credits.yangNote: Humphrey Yang's two TikTok videos (February 2020) used one grain of rice for 100,000 $ and ended with about 58 pounds of rice for Jeff Bezos' 122 billion. The rice chapter uses his scale by default.
credits.agarwalNote: Neal Agarwal's ‘Spend Bill Gates' Money’ (2017) is the template for the spend simulator. Ours adds public-good items, sourced prices and inflation adjustment.
credits.otherFormats: We looked for further widely known originals of these formats. The ‘spend the money’ idea has many clones of neal.fun; the rice idea has been repeated by others after Yang; we found no earlier originals to credit.
